newsitem.title: UK: Rouble reform boon to confidence -London analysts.
newsitem.headline: Rouble reform boon to confidence -London analysts.

text.p: Plans to slash three zeros off the Russian rouble is neutral for the currency's value on the foreign exchanges but will enhance confidence in Russia's fight against inflation, London-based analysts said.
The rouble reforms, announced earlier on Monday, will take place at the beginning of 1998 and will mean that one new rouble will be worth 1,000 old ones, or 17 cents at current rates.
Analysts said the net impact of the move will be felt internally by making big-ticket transactions less unwieldy in roubles, rendering the use of dollars for these purposes less attractive.
The biggest rouble note in circulation at present is 500,000, or about $86.
A greater willingness to hold the domestic currency will help dampen inflationary expectations further, analysts said.

"For foreign investors this move is fairly neutral but in the bigger picture it's a tangible sign of Russia's success in reducing inflation," said David Boren, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.

The government is forecasting inflation will dip to 11 percent this year as a whole from about 14.5 percent in June and 22 percent in 1996. Inflation had soared to more than 1,000 percent in the early 1990s and the rouble collapsed as reform of the former Soviet economy got underway.
"It's all about confidence. Theoretically the redenomination will have no effect on the rouble's external value," said Joe Prendergast, head of currency strategy at CSFB.
After an initial flurry of rouble sales on the announcement, the unit steadied quickly and at midday in Europe was little changed from Friday at 5801/03 per dollar.
Foreign demand for Russian government debt has soared over the past year as inflation slowed and attractive yields on Treasury bills - currently about 18 percent - began to slide.
Analysts said the rouble reform is a signal from the government that it is confident that a tight monetary policy and stable rouble regime would be maintained.
Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin said Monday that Russian currency policy remains unchanged and the rouble will continue to devalue roughly in line with inflation next year.
"I don't see any reason for a dramatic change in currency policy for 1998. The gradual devaluation of the rouble will most likely continue in line with inflation," Dubinin said.

Since mid-1995 the central bank has held the rouble in a pre-announced currency band allowing a gradual devaluation. The mechanism is similar to a crawling peg devaluation but with an upper and lower limit rather than a central peg.

The rouble has never moved outside the corridor limits and has only rarely strayed outside the central bank's own rates. The corridor will end the year at 5,750-6,350 per dollar after starting it at 5,500-6,100.
"Probably the government's biggest problem with the reform will be ensuring that the domestic population understands exactly what it means," said Boren at Salomon.
The last redenomination of the rouble took place in 1991, when people were given just three days to exchange the notes and a panic ensued.
This time around existing notes will be legal tender until the end of the 1998. ($ = 5800 Russian Roubles)
